# APUSH Timeline 2026: All 9 Periods, Key Events & Themes


**TL;DR:** The APUSH timeline spans 1491 to the present, divided into 9 periods by the College Board. Units 3 through 8 (1754 to 1980) account for roughly 80% of the exam. You don’t need to memorize hundreds of exact dates. Instead, learn the period framework, nail about 15 to 20 anchor dates, and trace the 8 course themes across those periods. Starting in 2027, all short-answer and long essay questions are required, so you can no longer skip weak periods.


---


The APUSH timeline is the backbone of every AP US History exam. It organizes 530+ years of American history into nine testable periods, each with its own date range, themes, and weight on the exam. But most timeline resources online are just massive event dumps with no indication of what actually matters for scoring.


This guide is different. It pairs every period with its exam weight, explains why periods overlap, maps the 8 APUSH themes to specific eras, and gives you a curated shortlist of dates worth memorizing. Think of it as the one reference page that replaces the ten browser tabs you currently have open.


If you’re juggling APUSH alongside SAT or ACT prep, a[free diagnostic test](https://miyagilabs.ai/sat/diagnostic-test) can help you identify weak spots on the standardized test side so you can allocate study time more efficiently.


---


## What Is the APUSH Timeline?


The APUSH timeline is the College Board’s chronological framework for AP US History. It divides American history from 1491 (pre-Columbian contact) to the present into 9 distinct periods. Each period represents a major era defined by dominant political, economic, social, and cultural forces.


The exam doesn’t treat all periods equally. Some carry 10 to 17% of the total score, while others carry as little as 4 to 6%. Understanding this weighting is critical for smart studying.


A few key facts about the exam itself:


- Approximately[517,000 students](https://www.albert.io/blog/ap-us-history-faq/) took APUSH in 2025, making it one of the most popular AP exams.
- On the 2026 exam, 74% of students scored a 3 or higher and 14% earned a 5.
- Since May 2025, APUSH is fully digital through College Board’s Bluebook app. All sections, including the DBQ and LEQ essays, are typed.


The exam tests four historical thinking skills: causation, comparison, contextualization, and argumentation. Raw date recall matters far less than your ability to[place events in context and build arguments](https://apushscorecalculator.us/apush-exam-guide) . That’s why a smart APUSH timeline focuses on interpretation, not memorization.


---


## The 9 APUSH Periods at a Glance


Here’s the master reference table. Bookmark this. Print it. Tape it to your wall.


Period Date Range Exam Weight Dominant Theme(s) Anchor Events


1 1491–1607 4–6% MIG, WOR, GEO Columbian Exchange, Spanish conquests, Native civilizations


2 1607–1754 6–8% MIG, SOC, WXT Jamestown (1607), Atlantic slave trade expansion, Great Awakening


3 1754–1800 10–17% PCE, NAT, WOR French and Indian War, Declaration of Independence (1776), Constitutional Convention (1787)


4 1800–1848 10–17% PCE, WXT, GEO Louisiana Purchase, Market Revolution, Jacksonian Democracy, Mexican-American War


5 1844–1877 10–17% PCE, SOC, NAT Compromise of 1850, Civil War (1861–1865), Reconstruction Amendments


6 1865–1898 10–17% WXT, MIG, SOC Transcontinental Railroad, Gilded Age industrialization, Plessy v. Ferguson (1896)


7 1890–1945 10–17% WOR, PCE, WXT Progressive Era, WWI, Great Depression (1929), New Deal, WWII/Pearl Harbor (1941)


8 1945–1980 10–17% WOR, SOC, ARC Cold War, Civil Rights Movement (1954–1965), Vietnam War, Great Society


9 1980–Present 4–6% PCE, WOR, WXT Reagan Revolution, end of Cold War, 9/11, tech economy


**The critical takeaway:**[Units 3 through 8](https://www.savemyexams.com/learning-hub/subject-guides/ap-us-history-units/) cover 1754 to 1980 and make up about 80% of exam questions. Units 1, 2, and 9 account for the remaining 20%. Your study time should reflect this ratio.


### Why Do the Periods Overlap?


This confuses almost every APUSH student, and it’s not a typo. Period 4 ends in 1848 but Period 5 starts in 1844. Period 5 runs to 1877 while Period 6 begins in 1865. Period 6 ends in 1898 but Period 7 starts in 1890.


The overlap is intentional. Real historical transitions don’t have clean cutoffs.[Reconstruction and the rise of industry happened simultaneously](https://histlgame.com/apush-periods) , so they belong to both the Period 5 and Period 6 stories. Westward expansion and the intensifying slavery debate predated secession, which is why Period 5 starts before the Civil War actually began.


For exam purposes, events in overlap zones are natural comparison-essay targets. If a DBQ asks you to analyze change over time from 1860 to 1900, you’re working squarely in the Period 5/6 overlap, and understanding both narratives simultaneously is what earns you points.


---


## Period-by-Period APUSH Timeline Glossary


### Period 1: 1491–1607 (4–6% of Exam)


**Main change:** European contact transforms the Americas. **Main conflict:** Collision between Native, European, and eventually African peoples and cultures.


Year/Era Event Why It Matters


Pre-1492 Diverse Native civilizations (Pueblo, Mississippian, Iroquois) Establishes that the Americas had complex societies before European arrival


1492 Columbus reaches the Caribbean Launches the Columbian Exchange


1490s–1600s Columbian Exchange Transfer of crops, animals, diseases, and ideas between hemispheres; decimation of Native populations


1500s Spanish conquests (Aztec, Inca) First European colonial empires in the Americas; encomienda system


1500s–1600s Spanish mission system Early attempts at cultural and religious conversion


**Dominant themes:** MIG (Migration and Settlement), WOR (America in the World), GEO (Geography and the Environment)


**Common essay angle:** Compare the effects of European contact on different Native groups, or analyze how the Columbian Exchange reshaped global trade networks.


---


### Period 2: 1607–1754 (6–8% of Exam)


**Main change:** Permanent English colonies take root along the Atlantic coast. **Main conflict:** Tensions between colonial self-governance and imperial control, plus the entrenchment of racial slavery.


Year/Era Event Why It Matters


1607 Jamestown founded First permanent English settlement; establishes cash-crop economy (tobacco)


1619 First Africans arrive in Virginia Beginning of African slavery in English North America


1620 Plymouth Colony (Pilgrims) Religious dissent as a motive for colonization


1630s Massachusetts Bay Colony Puritan “city upon a hill” ideal; shapes New England identity


1676 Bacon’s Rebellion Exposes class tensions; accelerates shift toward racial slavery


1730s–1740s Great Awakening First mass religious revival; unifies colonists across regions


**Dominant themes:** MIG, SOC (Social Structures), WXT (Work, Exchange, and Technology)


**Common essay angle:** Analyze how labor systems evolved in the Chesapeake vs. New England colonies, or explain how the Great Awakening laid groundwork for revolutionary ideas.


---


### Period 3: 1754–1800 (10–17% of Exam)


**Main change:** Colonies break from Britain and create a new constitutional republic. **Main conflict:** Balancing liberty with order, and defining who counts as a citizen.


Year/Era Event Why It Matters


1754–1763 French and Indian War Britain wins but incurs massive debt, leading to new colonial taxes


1765 Stamp Act Sparks “no taxation without representation”


1773 Boston Tea Party Escalation of colonial resistance


1776 Declaration of Independence Formally breaks ties with Britain; articulates Enlightenment ideals


1781 Articles of Confederation ratified First US government, intentionally weak


1787 Constitutional Convention Creates the Constitution; Great Compromise, Three-Fifths Compromise


1791 Bill of Rights ratified Protects individual liberties; addresses Anti-Federalist concerns


**Dominant themes:** PCE (Politics and Power), NAT (American and National Identity), WOR


**Common essay angle:** Compare Federalist and Anti-Federalist arguments, or evaluate how revolutionary ideals applied unevenly to women, enslaved people, and Native Americans.


---


### Period 4: 1800–1848 (10–17% of Exam)


**Main change:** The nation expands westward and develops a market economy. **Main conflict:** Sectional tensions over slavery intensify as new territory is acquired.


Year/Era Event Why It Matters


1803 Louisiana Purchase Doubles the nation’s size; raises constitutional questions about federal power


1812–1815 War of 1812 Boosts American nationalism; weakens Native resistance in the West


1820 Missouri Compromise Temporarily settles slavery expansion debate at 36°30’ line


1820s–1840s Market Revolution Canals, railroads, and factories transform the economy


1828 Andrew Jackson elected Rise of mass democracy and the “common man” narrative


1830 Indian Removal Act Forced relocation of southeastern Native nations (Trail of Tears)


1848 Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo / Seneca Falls Convention Vast territory acquired from Mexico; women’s rights movement begins


**Dominant themes:** PCE, WXT, GEO


**Common essay angle:** Analyze how westward expansion made the sectional crisis over slavery worse, or compare economic development in the North and South.


---


### Period 5: 1844–1877 (10–17% of Exam)


**Main change:** The slavery crisis erupts into Civil War, followed by Reconstruction. **Main conflict:** Can the Union survive, and what does freedom mean for formerly enslaved people?


Year/Era Event Why It Matters


1850 Compromise of 1850 Includes Fugitive Slave Act; deepens sectional anger


1854 Kansas-Nebraska Act Overturns Missouri Compromise; leads to “Bleeding Kansas”


1857 Dred Scott v. Sandford Supreme Court rules African Americans are not citizens


1861–1865 Civil War Deadliest American conflict; decides the slavery question by force


1863 Emancipation Proclamation Redefines the war as a fight against slavery


1865 13th Amendment ratified Abolishes slavery


1865–1877 Reconstruction Attempts to rebuild the South and integrate freedpeople; ultimately undermined


**Dominant themes:** PCE, SOC, NAT


Most students find Period 5[among the most challenging](https://beaststudy.com/blog/how-to-study-for-apush/) because of the density of causes, consequences, and primary sources.


**Common essay angle:** Evaluate the successes and failures of Reconstruction, or trace how debates over slavery evolved from compromise to conflict.


---


### Period 6: 1865–1898 (10–17% of Exam)


**Main change:** Rapid industrialization, urbanization, and western settlement transform the nation. **Main conflict:** How should government respond to monopolies, labor unrest, and racial inequality?


Year/Era Event Why It Matters


1869 Transcontinental Railroad completed Links East and West; accelerates settlement and economic growth


1870s–1890s Gilded Age Massive wealth inequality; rise of Carnegie, Rockefeller, and Morgan


1876 Battle of Little Bighorn Symbolic last major Native military victory; followed by reservation system


1882 Chinese Exclusion Act First federal law restricting immigration by nationality


1886 Haymarket Affair Highlights labor unrest and anti-union backlash


1890 Wounded Knee Massacre End of the Indian Wars


1896 Plessy v. Ferguson “Separate but equal” doctrine legalizes segregation


**Dominant themes:** WXT, MIG, SOC


**Common essay angle:** Compare responses to industrialization from workers, farmers (Populists), and business leaders.


---


### Period 7: 1890–1945 (10–17% of Exam)


**Main change:** The US becomes a global power through war and economic expansion. **Main conflict:** Balancing reform at home with involvement abroad.


This is[one of the most content-dense periods](https://cognito.org/blog/apush-units-guide/) on the entire exam.


Year/Era Event Why It Matters


1898 Spanish-American War US acquires overseas territories; debates imperialism


1900s–1920 Progressive Era Reform movements target corruption, labor conditions, and women’s suffrage


1914–1918 World War I (US enters 1917) Expands federal power; suppresses dissent (Sedition Act)


1920 19th Amendment Women gain the right to vote


1929 Stock market crash Triggers the Great Depression


1933–1939 New Deal FDR expands federal government’s role in the economy


1941 Pearl Harbor attack US enters World War II


The[Great Depression and New Deal](https://beaststudy.com/blog/how-to-study-for-apush/) are among the most frequently tested topics on the entire exam. Don’t skim them.


**Dominant themes:** WOR, PCE, WXT


**Common essay angle:** Analyze the extent to which the New Deal represented a turning point in the role of the federal government.


---


### Period 8: 1945–1980 (10–17% of Exam)


**Main change:** Cold War shapes foreign and domestic policy while social movements reshape American society. **Main conflict:** How far should equality extend, and what role should the US play globally?


Year/Era Event Why It Matters


1947 Truman Doctrine Establishes containment as US Cold War strategy


1950–1953 Korean War First “hot” conflict of the Cold War


1954 Brown v. Board of Education Overturns “separate but equal”; launches modern Civil Rights era


1955–1965 Civil Rights Movement core years Montgomery Bus Boycott, March on Washington, Civil Rights Act (1964), Voting Rights Act (1965)


1964–1968 Great Society programs Medicare, Medicaid, War on Poverty


1965–1973 Vietnam War (major US involvement) Divides the nation; fuels antiwar movement


1972 Watergate break-in Leads to Nixon’s resignation; erodes trust in government


**Dominant themes:** WOR, SOC, ARC (American and Regional Culture)


**Common essay angle:** Compare the strategies of the Civil Rights Movement (nonviolent protest vs. Black Power), or evaluate the impact of the Cold War on domestic policy.


---


### Period 9: 1980–Present (4–6% of Exam)


**Main change:** Conservative resurgence, globalization, and the digital revolution reshape America. **Main conflict:** Culture wars, the role of government, and America’s place in a post-Cold War world.


Year/Era Event Why It Matters


1980 Reagan elected Conservative movement gains power; tax cuts, deregulation


1989–1991 Fall of Berlin Wall / Soviet collapse End of the Cold War


1990–1991 Gulf War First post-Cold War military action


2001 September 11 attacks War on Terror begins; Patriot Act expands surveillance


2008 Financial crisis Worst recession since the Great Depression; government bailouts


**Dominant themes:** PCE, WOR, WXT


**Common essay angle:** Evaluate the extent of the “conservative revolution” under Reagan, or analyze how 9/11 changed US foreign policy.


---


## The 8 APUSH Themes and How They Thread the Timeline


Every DBQ and LEQ prompt is anchored to at least one of[eight course themes](https://fiveable.me/apush/thematic-guides/theme-8-social-structures/study-guide/3w8l3oMqcUE0RRzAKxCx) . These themes run through all nine periods. Learning to trace a single theme across the entire APUSH timeline is the core skill for writing strong essays.


Use the **SPACEMEN** mnemonic to remember them:


Letter Theme What It Covers


S SOC: Social Structures Class, race, gender, ethnicity, and how hierarchies form and change


P PCE: Politics and Power Government systems, political parties, civic participation, reform


A WOR: America in the World Diplomacy, war, trade, immigration, and the US role globally


C ARC: American and Regional Culture Art, religion, philosophy, education, popular culture


E GEO: Geography and the Environment Land use, resource extraction, environmental consequences


M MIG: Migration and Settlement Why and how people move, from colonization to modern immigration


E WXT: Work, Exchange, and Technology Labor, capitalism, innovation, and economic systems


N NAT: American and National Identity Who is “American,” national ideals, debates over inclusion


### Quick Theme-to-Period Crosswalk


- **WOR** peaks in Periods 1, 3, 7, and 8 (contact, revolution, world wars, Cold War)
- **SOC** is most testable in Periods 2, 5, 6, and 8 (slavery, Reconstruction, Gilded Age, Civil Rights)
- **PCE** is heavy in Periods 3, 4, 5, and 9 (founding, Jacksonian era, Civil War politics, conservative movement)
- **WXT** dominates Periods 4, 6, and 7 (Market Revolution, industrialization, Depression/New Deal)


When you study the APUSH timeline, don’t just memorize events in isolation. Ask yourself: which themes does this event connect to? That question is exactly what essay prompts are testing.


---


## Which Dates Do You Actually Need to Memorize?


Here’s the good news:[the exam rewards decade-level placement and reasoning](https://ingeniusprep.com/blog/ap-us-history-study-tips/) , not rote recall of specific days. You need to place events in the right period and explain their significance. You do not need to know that the Battle of Gettysburg happened on July 1 to 3, 1863. You need to know it was a Civil War turning point in the early 1860s.


That said, certain anchor dates appear constantly across MCQ, SAQ, DBQ, and LEQ prompts. Here’s a curated shortlist of roughly 20 dates worth committing to memory:


**Must-Know APUSH Anchor Dates:**


1. **1492** — Columbus arrives; Columbian Exchange begins
2. **1607** — Jamestown founded
3. **1676** — Bacon’s Rebellion
4. **1754** — French and Indian War begins
5. **1776** — Declaration of Independence
6. **1787** — Constitutional Convention
7. **1803** — Louisiana Purchase
8. **1820** — Missouri Compromise
9. **1830** — Indian Removal Act
10. **1848** — Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo / Seneca Falls
11. **1861–1865** — Civil War
12. **1865–1877** — Reconstruction
13. **1896** — Plessy v. Ferguson
14. **1898** — Spanish-American War
15. **1917** — US enters WWI
16. **1929** — Stock market crash
17. **1933** — New Deal begins
18. **1941** — Pearl Harbor
19. **1954** — Brown v. Board of Education
20. **1964–1965** — Civil Rights Act / Voting Rights Act


Study advice from the OnePrep blog recommends building the nine-period framework first, then choosing[2 to 4 anchor dates per period](https://www.oneprep.com/blog/how-to-remember-dates-for-apush-without-stress) rather than attempting to memorize exhaustive lists. This approach matches how the exam actually tests you.


### The Two-Sentence Summary Method


A practical technique recommended by multiple study guides: write a two-sentence summary for each period. One sentence explains the main change. The other explains the main conflict. This forces you to prioritize interpretation over memorization, which is exactly the skill the exam rewards.


For example, Period 7: “The US became a global superpower through two world wars while expanding federal power at home through Progressive reforms and the New Deal. The central conflict was balancing domestic reform with growing international obligations.”


If you can do this for all nine periods from memory, you have a strong working framework for any essay prompt.

## APUSH Exam Format and 2027 Changes That Affect Timeline Study


### Current Format (2025–2026)


Section Questions Time Score Weight


Multiple Choice 55 questions 55 minutes 40%


Short Answer (SAQ) 3 questions 40 minutes 20%


Document-Based Question (DBQ) 1 essay 60 minutes (includes reading time) 25%


Long Essay Question (LEQ) 1 essay (chosen from options) 40 minutes 15%


### What Changes in 2027


The May 2027 exam introduces a[redesigned short-answer and long-essay section](https://itutoronline.com/blog/ap-us-history-exam-2027) . Two major shifts:


1.


**All three SAQs are required.** In 2026, you answered questions 1 and 2, then chose between question 3 or 4. Starting in 2027, all three are mandatory, each covering a different period between 1491 and 2001.


2.


**One required LEQ prompt.** In 2026, you chose one of three prompts. In 2027, there’s a single required prompt covering roughly half the course’s time periods.


**What this means for timeline study:** You can no longer dodge your weakest periods. If Period 6 (Gilded Age) has always been a blind spot, the 2027 format could hand you an SAQ on exactly that era with no escape hatch. Timeline mastery across all periods becomes non-negotiable.


For students also preparing for the SAT, structuring your study time is everything. A[study plan generator](https://miyagilabs.ai/sat/study-plan-generator) can help you build a schedule that balances both exams without burning out.

## How to Use an APUSH Timeline to Study


Knowing the timeline exists isn’t the same as using it effectively. Here are concrete strategies.


### 1. Start with the Framework, Not the Details


Before you memorize a single date, make sure you can name all nine periods, their approximate date ranges, and one sentence about what each period is “about.” This skeleton gives every future fact a place to attach.


### 2. Allocate Time by Exam Weight


Periods 3 through 8 make up roughly 80% of the exam. If you have 20 hours to study, spend about 16 of those on Periods 3 through 8 and only 4 on Periods 1, 2, and 9. This is the highest-return time allocation.


### 3. Trace One Theme Across All Nine Periods


Pick a theme like WXT (Work, Exchange, and Technology). Then walk through the timeline: What was the economy like in Period 1? How did it change by Period 4 (Market Revolution)? What happened in Period 6 (industrialization)? Period 7 (Depression and New Deal)?


This exercise is the single best way to prepare for LEQ and DBQ essays. Every prompt asks you to make an argument about change or continuity over time, and tracing themes is how you build that argument.


### 4. Use Practice Questions, Not Just Flashcards


Flashcards test recognition. Exam questions test application. After reviewing a period, immediately try MCQ or SAQ questions from that era. Active recall under test conditions beats passive review every time. If you’re looking for[structured practice resources](https://miyagilabs.ai/sat/practice-questions) for standardized tests, the same principle applies.


### 5. Focus on Overlap Zones for Essay Practice


Events that sit in overlapping periods (Reconstruction, early Progressive Era, Gilded Age/imperialism transition) are prime essay material because they naturally invite comparison and change-over-time analysis. Spend extra time on these transition points.


### 6. Pay Special Attention to the Hardest Periods


Periods 5 and 7 consistently give students the most trouble. Period 5 because the causes and consequences of the Civil War are dense. Period 7 because it packs the Progressive Era, two world wars, and the Great Depression into a single unit. Don’t leave these for last.


For students managing multiple standardized tests simultaneously, exploring[AP study resources](https://miyagilabs.ai/blog/best-ap-study-resources) can help you find the right tools for each exam.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### What is the APUSH timeline?


The APUSH timeline is the College Board’s chronological framework for AP US History, spanning 1491 to the present. It divides American history into 9 periods, each defined by major political, economic, social, and cultural developments. The timeline serves as the organizational backbone of the course and exam.


### How many periods are in APUSH?


There are 9 periods. They range from Period 1 (1491–1607) through Period 9 (1980–present). Periods 3 through 8 carry the heaviest exam weight at 10 to 17% each.


### Do APUSH periods overlap?


Yes, and it’s intentional. Period 4 ends in 1848 but Period 5 starts in 1844. Period 5 ends in 1877 but Period 6 starts in 1865. Period 6 ends in 1898 but Period 7 starts in 1890. These overlaps reflect the reality that historical transitions are gradual, not instantaneous. Events in overlap zones frequently appear in comparison essays.


### Do I need to memorize exact dates for APUSH?


No. The exam tests your ability to place events in the correct period and decade, then explain their significance. You should know roughly 15 to 20 anchor dates (like 1776, 1787, 1861–1865, 1929, 1941) but don’t need to memorize specific days or months for most events.


### What are the hardest APUSH periods?


Most students find Periods 5 (Civil War and Reconstruction) and 7 (Progressive Era through World War II) the most difficult because of their density and complexity. Period 7 in particular covers more than half a century of rapid change. The Great Depression and New Deal are among the most frequently tested topics across the entire exam.


### What are the 8 APUSH themes?


The themes are: Social Structures (SOC), Politics and Power (PCE), America in the World (WOR), American and Regional Culture (ARC), Geography and the Environment (GEO), Migration and Settlement (MIG), Work, Exchange, and Technology (WXT), and American and National Identity (NAT). Use the SPACEMEN mnemonic to remember them.


### What changed on the APUSH exam for 2027?


Starting in May 2027, all three short-answer questions are required (no more choosing between options), and there is one required long essay prompt instead of a choice of three. This means students must have working knowledge of all nine periods. You can no longer avoid weak areas.


### How should I study the APUSH timeline?


Build the nine-period framework first. Then add 2 to 4 anchor dates per period. Practice tracing themes across all periods for essay prep. Allocate study time proportionally to exam weight (80% on Periods 3 through 8). Use practice questions rather than passive review to test your recall.


---


Mastering the APUSH timeline isn’t about memorizing every date in American history. It’s about understanding the structure, knowing what the exam prioritizes, and being able to connect events across periods and themes. With the 2027 changes removing the option to skip weak periods, breadth matters more than ever.


If you’re balancing APUSH with SAT prep, take a[free SAT practice test](https://miyagilabs.ai/sat/practice-tests) to see where you stand and build a study plan that covers both exams without spreading yourself too thin.
